title: Indigo→violet gradient
summary: The #6366f1→#a855f7 (indigo→purple/violet) diagonal on buttons, glows and hero backgrounds is the factory setting of Tailwind demos; it reads as an absence of a decision. Only a genuine brand in that hue escapes.
notes: Purpose-gate: a purple brand or a one-off illustration is fine; slop is the combination purple gradient + glow + pill button as the unchosen default.

title: Gradient headline text
summary: background-clip:text rainbow fills on headings trade legibility for an effect every AI page uses. Hallmark: no genre allows gradient text; solid ink for headings, hierarchy from size/weight/space.

source.rule: Gate 2 — No genre allows gradient text
Bans — no gradient text on headings

notes: A logo wordmark is the usual legitimate exception; a single deliberate hero treatment may be defended.

title: Warm 'cozy' palette
summary: An amber/stone/orange wash on soft beige is the model's laziest translation of 'warm and friendly' — Tailwind's warm ramp served raw so every 'human' product looks identical.
notes: False positives: food/coffee/craft brands where warm is the identity. The last pattern is the sibling tell — default gray text dropped onto a tinted surface was never toned to its background.

title: Default semantic palette
summary: Info in blue/indigo, tip in amber, success in green, error in red — the framework's stock -50 backgrounds with -600 text — is a bowl of unrelated rainbow candy when three or four pairs are used together with no brand link.

tests.label: three stock semantic pairs together fail
tests.input:
Info
Tip
Done

notes: Grow semantic colors out of one palette (tints of a hue plus neutrals); colour only the states that truly differ. A single deliberate status colour is fine.

title: One-hue status box
summary: An alert whose border, text and /10 background are all one hue (border-red-500 / text-red-500 / bg-red-500/10) is a traffic light, not a palette — one loud hue at three opacities, nothing toned to sit next to the UI.

tests.label: red-on-red alert fails
tests.input: Error

tests.label: muted accent on neutral passes
tests.input: Error

notes: Carry the state in words and weight first; if you colour, one muted accent from your own palette on a neutral surface.

title: Gradients as atmosphere
summary: Page-wide radial glows, card surfaces that are themselves top-to-bottom gradients, per-card accent-hue washes and repeating-gradient stripes carry no information — the default 'premium dark mode' move.

tests.label: radial glow behind everything fails
tests.input: body { background: radial-gradient(circle at 50% 0%, rgba(139,92,246,0.15), transparent 60%); }

notes: A gradient that points at something specific (responds to interaction, separates hierarchy) is a choice; build surface depth with a hairline and a restrained shadow instead.

title: Pure #000 / #fff base
summary: Exact #FFFFFF on exact #000000 is harsh, cold and reads as unfinished; toned whites and blacks (#FAFAFA / #1A1A1A) are softer and more professional.

source.rule: Rule 6 Color — subtly toned whites and blacks

tests.label: pure black on pure white fails

notes: Genre note: modern-minimal allows pure #fff paper (Stripe / ElevenLabs school).

title: Zero-chroma neutrals
summary: A neutral/surface color with zero chroma in oklch (oklch(... 0 ...)) reads flat; tint every neutral toward the anchor hue — minimum 0.005 chroma.
notes: Genre note: modern-minimal allows zero-chroma neutrals (the monochrome Stripe / ElevenLabs school).

title: Palette overflow (5+ colors)
summary: A scattered palette has no hierarchy; cap the active palette at 2–3 core colors + 1 accent (neutrals excluded). When every element can be any color, nothing is distinguished.

source.rule: Too Many Colors in the Palette

notes: Count distinct color values on one page; neutral greys/whites/blacks do not count toward the core palette.

title: Mid-render token improvisation
summary: Inline hex/oklch/rgb/hsl values or font-family declarations outside the token block mean the model picked a theme then freestyled — cohesion erodes into eight colors instead of three.

source.rule: Rule 7 Color values — trace to a token
R-31 Every decision must have a reason

notes: Every color/font must reference a named token (var(--color-accent), font-family: var(--font-display)); lift needed values into the token block first. Flags hit only outside the token definitions.

title: Off-scale spacing values
summary: Padding/margin/gap values that are not multiples of 4 or 8 (padding: 17px, gap: 13px) feel chaotic; snap spacing to a named scale (multiples of 4px/8px).

source.rule: Rule 8 Spacing — snap to a 4px/8px scale

notes: Regex flags common off-scale values; engines may implement a divisibility check instead. A deliberate one-off (e.g. optical centering) may be defended.

title: Excessive accent coverage
summary: One accent color on buttons, icons, badges, links, lines, backgrounds and glows at once — or an accent covering more than ~5% of a viewport — stops being an accent; the design loses its focal point.

tests.label: accent on every element fails
tests.input: Hero title, all four buttons, all feature icons, badge and footer links all painted in the same brand accent.

tests.label: accent on primary CTA only passes
tests.input: Accent appears once, on the primary CTA; everything else uses neutrals and one ink.

notes: Zero accents is sterile; an accent everywhere is slop. Choose the one or two places it matters.

title: Dark mode default without reason
summary: An entire page is dark just because it looks 'tech', with no branding consideration; dark is a decision, not a default. Developer/creative tools have legitimate reasons; content-first products usually do not.

source.rule: Dark Mode Default for No Reason

tests.label: dark-only fintech landing fails
tests.input: Fintech consumer landing page ships dark-only because 'dark looks tech', with no brand or audience reason.

tests.label: dev tool dark default passes
tests.input: Terminal/developer tool ships dark default and documents why (code-heavy UI, user preference).

notes: If the product has no strong reason for a fixed theme, build a working light/dark toggle — a theme toggle you ship must work in both modes.

title: Background grid
summary: Grid squares, blueprint lines and graph paper are the default way to make a flat page feel 'technical' without doing real work — texture without intent.
notes: Use texture or pattern only when it genuinely supports the product's identity, with the reason written down; a real identity motif beats a stock grid.

title: Banned default typefaces (Inter & co.)
summary: Inter, Roboto, Open Sans, Lato, Poppins, Manrope, Space Grotesk, Geist and friends are on-distribution for every LLM; a typeface is the loudest single signal of who made this, and defaulting to the training-data average dodges the identity decision.

matcher.pattern: fonts\.googleapis\.com/css2\?family=(Inter|Space\+Grotesk|Manrope|Plus\+Jakarta)|font-family:\s*[^;]*(Inter|Roboto|Open Sans|Lato|Poppins|Montserrat|Raleway|Work Sans|DM Sans|Nunito|Manrope|Plus Jakarta Sans|Space Grotesk|Geist|Arial|Helvetica)|from ["']next/font/google

source.rule: Rule 5 Type — fonts chosen with intent

notes: Purpose-gate: landing back on Inter after comparing alternatives is a choice; starting there isn't. A system stack picked for a reason is also a choice. Same family at different weights counts as one face.

title: Serif-italic on one word in a heading
summary: Swapping one word in a sans headline to serif italic is the most viral AI headline tic — cheap drama staging two voices in one sentence; headers are roman, emphasis comes from weight, accent colour, or a drawn underline.

tests.label: italic emphasis word inside sans h1 fails
italic emphasis in body paragraph passes

notes: Emphasise with weight, position or a line break; keep one voice, and if italic is truly needed use the same family's italic. Italic is allowed only as body-copy emphasis inside running paragraphs.

title: Serif where sans belongs
summary: Playfair/Lora/Cormorant display serif on a dev tool or SaaS — as body/UI text or an oversized italic-serif hero — is a tuxedo on a terminal; display serifs are hard to read at UI sizes and tonally off.

source.rule: Rule 9 editorial-warm — serif display faces as silent defaults

tests.label: Playfair on a SaaS hero fails
tests.input: .hero h1 { font-family: "Playfair Display", serif; font-style: italic; }

tests.label: serif on genuine editorial content passes

notes: False positives: an editorial/publishing product that wants serif. Set the hero roman or use a non-serif display face; a genuinely editorial register may keep it.

title: Decorative strikes & highlights
summary: Striking out, underlining, or highlighter-swipe over words not to delete/annotate but as decorative 'emphasis' means the design doesn't trust the words; keep strike for real edits, underline for links, highlight for real annotation.

source.rule: Gate 35 decorative text effects positioned correctly

tests.label: decorative strikethrough on a keyword fails
tests.input: We are not another AI wrapper

notes: Real edits (<del> in a changelog), links (underline) and annotations (<mark>) are the confirmation pass; the regex fires on all strikes and the triage confirms the decoration-vs-annotation distinction. A highlighter band must sit behind the x-height, never at the baseline.

title: Kicker above every heading
summary: A tiny uppercase letter-spaced label restating the heading (FEATURES over features) is an editorial device worn as a reflex — zero information, a template's rhythm; a kicker earns its place only when it adds a real dimension (category, date, number in a sequence).

source.rule: R-06 Typography (uppercase labels with extreme letter-spacing)

tests.label: kicker adding a real dimension passes
tests.input:
Issue 12 · October

The October Review

notes: Delete any kicker that restates its heading; keep one only where it adds a real dimension, capped at 1–2 per page, heading directly underneath in the same column.

title: Tag-left / header-right section heads
summary: An eyebrow or ordinal in a narrow left column beside the section title (01 · THE TOUR | Features) is the single most reliable AI-templated tell for editorial-style SaaS pages; eyebrows stack vertically under the heading or not at all.

source.rule: Eyebrow on every section — hard ban

tests.label: two-column section head fails
tests.input: .section__head { grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr; } — '01 / EXAMPLES' in the left column, the title to its right.

tests.label: vertical stack passes
tests.input: Eyebrow sits directly above the heading in the same column; no two-column section-head grid.

notes: Not bypassable by parity instructions: even when asked to 'match the existing structure', drop the pattern and flatten the head to single column.

title: Full-sentence display headline
summary: A whole marketing sentence set at display size (text-6xl font-extrabold tracking-tight) wraps to three or four lines and eats the viewport; display sizes are for the two or three words that can carry that scale. Cap display at 5.5rem (88px).

source.rule: Hero headline sizing — 51+ chars step down; display ≤ 5.5rem

tests.label: sentence at display size fails
tests.input: The complete platform for modern teams who ship faster every single day

notes: Compress the one thing into a few words and let those be big; say the rest in a normal-size subline. A 100-char headline at display size is the single most reliable AI tell. Single-word displays ≤ 12 ch may grow to 7rem.

title: Flat type hierarchy
summary: Every size crammed between 14 and 18px — headings barely bigger than body, hierarchy left to shades of gray — is the safe play of nobody deciding what matters; use a scale with few steps and real contrast (1.25× and up).

source.rule: Chapter 7 Hierarchy — similar sizes flatten hierarchy

notes: If two sizes are within a pixel or two, merge them. A deliberately quiet single-size editorial layout with strong spacing is a choice; a dashboard where page title and table cell match is not.

title: More than three font families (2+1 rule)
summary: A page may use at most three distinct families: one display, one body, and an optional outlier for a single typographic moment. Four families is slop; mono counts as a face in any non-code context.

params.note: same family at different weights = 1; mono in non-code context = 1

source.rule: The 2+1 rule — three faces is the ceiling
Gate 37 more than three font families

tests.label: four families fail
tests.input: font-family: "Fraunces", serif; font-family: "Geist", sans-serif; font-family: "Geist Mono", monospace; font-family: "Anton", sans-serif;

notes: The outlier is a register, not a third surface: wordmark + hero stat is the canonical pair, never a fifth slot.

title: Prose measure outside 45–75ch
summary: Line length lives between 45 and 75 characters; under 45ch is choppy, over 75ch loses the eye. Default to max-width: 65ch.
notes: Regex flags any ch value < 45 or > 75; a deliberate narrow measure for captions or pull quotes may be defended.

title: Monospace as UI chrome ('tasteful terminal')
summary: Mono everywhere, near-black background, one warm accent, ASCII art — the look of 'an AI that read one Vercel blog post'. Keep monospace for code, not UI chrome; terminal metaphors only where they serve the product.

source.rule: R-06 Typography (large monospace for terminal aesthetics)

tests.label: mono on nav and hero copy fails
tests.input:
About · Pricing · Docs

Ship like a wizard

notes: Mono in code blocks and true terminal-aesthetic products are the confirmation pass; the tell is monospace on non-code UI chrome. Real taste is a choice you can explain, not this season's safest template.

title: Editorial dashboard
summary: An operational UI dressed as a magazine — giant serif 'Good evening' greeting, serif numerals in stat cards, cream paper, tracked-caps kickers — is the second-wave uniform; a console is scanned all day and needs legible sans with tabular lining numerals.

source.rule: Rule 9 editorial-warm on dashboards/dev tools is the default-template look

notes: Match the type to the job; display serif belongs to genuinely editorial surfaces (docs, essays, a magazine). For warmth, one material decision — a paper tint or an ink accent — not the full costume.

title: Icon-tile feature grid
summary: Three equal columns, each an icon-above-heading tile in a rounded-square chip — the shortest path to 'looks designed'; icons rarely relate to content, they just fill the grid. Break the grid, vary widths and heights, or drop the cards for typographic rhythm.

source.rule: Gate 3 3-equal-column card grid with icon-above-heading tiles

tests.label: 3-column icon tile grid fails
tests.input:
Speed

Go fast.

notes: An icon must carry meaning or go; a clear label + one sentence beats a row of glyphs. The giant decorative line icon (w-24 h-24) parked in a card is the same reflex at another size.

title: Cards inside cards
summary: A bordered rounded shadowed card holding another card holding another — three nested surfaces each with its own border/radius/shadow and shrinking padding — boxes because a box is the only grouping move the model trusts; one surface per region, group inside with spacing and hairlines.

source.rule: Gate 4 card nested inside another card

tests.label: three-deep nesting fails
tests.input: Content sliver

notes: A child earns its own surface only when it is genuinely a separate object (a preview, an embed).

title: Rounded card with colored left border
summary: A pale rounded box with a 4px colored bar down the left wrapped around every list item turns a docs admonition into universal decoration; the thick accent ring (border-2 in a loud color) is the sibling move. Callouts are scarce — one or two a page, only for a genuine aside.

source.rule: Rule 3 Cards — reserve border-left:4px for semantic emphasis

tests.label: callout style on every feature row fails
tests.input:
Feature A
Feature B

tests.label: one genuine tip callout passes
tests.input: <aside class="rounded-lg border border-amber-200 bg-amber-50 p-4">Tip: export before you delete.</aside>

notes: Let a list be a list — alignment, spacing, hierarchy. A hairline border all around, no border, or a small accent square beside the heading beats an asymmetric thick stripe.

title: Icon in a tint of itself
summary: Every icon wrapped in a rounded square filled with a 10% see-through tint of its own color (bg-blue-500/10 behind text-blue-600) turns the page into a grid of soft colored squares; let an icon just be an icon, inheriting the text color.

source.rule: 25 Icon in a tint of itself

notes: If something genuinely needs a container, give it a deliberate opaque surface from your palette, not a tint of the icon it holds.

title: Glassmorphism as default surface
summary: backdrop-blur panes on navbar, cards, modals and sidebar at once flatten every surface into the same frosted layer; glass is an accent that communicates depth over real content, not the character of the whole UI. Dose cap: 1–2 elements.
notes: Glass can work when it communicates depth (an overlay over content); it cannot work as decoration.

title: Pill-everything radius
summary: Every element max-radius — buttons, inputs, cards, badges, modals — erases the visual language of 'this is an input, this is a card'; radius becomes decoration instead of a hierarchy tool. Hold one small deliberate radius scale.

source.rule: R-11 Border Radius (not every element pill-shaped)

tests.label: pill card and pill input fail
tests.input: Card

notes: One generous radius on the primary CTA reads as intentional; the same radius on every element reads as a default. rounded-full on avatars and genuine pills only.

title: Oversized drop shadow
summary: A small card or icon under a huge, faint, barely-offset blur (60px+) is a fog, not a drop — a shadow says how high a surface floats, and this maps to no real height. Keep a small elevation scale: tight blur, small offset, low opacity, never a shadow bigger than the thing casting it.

tests.label: 60px blur on a small card fails

notes: The 'ghost card' variant — a hairline border plus a wide diffuse shadow on the same card — commits to two separators doing one job; pick an edge or an elevation, keep it colorless (a tinted glow is not depth).

title: Colored glow shadows / glow everywhere
summary: Colored box-shadow glows (shadow-indigo-500/40, 0 0 glows) used as dark-mode accents or on every card/button/icon/badge/background at once amplify nothing; glow is an attention amplifier reserved for 1–2 important elements as a focus accent.

tests.label: dark shadow on dark surface passes

notes: On dark surfaces, use elevation via lightness (brighter surface = higher), not shadow; if you must shadow, keep it tight and dark.

title: Corner craft: non-nesting radii / border dying at corner
summary: Two craft defects from radius-on-the-wrong-box: (a) an outer and inner box at the same big radius so corners don't sit concentrically (inner = outer − padding), and (b) a rounded overflow-hidden wrapper whose child owns the 1px border, erasing the stroke at every corner. Put radius and border on the same box.

source.rule: 22 The border that dies at the corner

notes: Grep gives leads; the break is visual — confirm in the rendered DOM. Nested radius = outer − padding, or don't round the inner element at all; a single flat radius scale that nests correctly is fine.

title: Badge & pill spam
summary: '✨ New', 'β Beta', '🔥 Popular' decorative pills everywhere manufacture fake buzz; in bulk each stops meaning anything. A badge is for real status only — a version, a stock level — never the capsule + thin border + glow + dot + uppercase combination.

tests.label: three decorative pills fail
tests.input: ✨ New🔥 Popular🚀 Launch

notes: A badge that reports a real, changing state (version, stock) is information; a badge that performs excitement is decoration.

title: Glowing status dot
summary: A status indicator drawn as a saturated green dot in a pale pulsing halo (animate-ping/pulse) inflates a binary state into a glowing gem; a status is a tiny signal — a small flat single-color dot plus a word, no halo, no pulse, and no dot at all if nothing is live behind it.

tests.label: pulsing halo status fails
tests.input: Live

tests.label: flat dot plus word passes
tests.input: Online

notes: Colour only when the state actually matters or changes — and if nothing is live behind it, no dot at all.

title: All-caps card grid
summary: An ALL-CAPS label plus a number or icon copied into rows of interchangeable cards fakes structure while stuffing unrelated things into identical boxes; the ALL-CAPS micro-label is the default costume for 'looks designed'. Decide the single most important thing and show it fully.

tests.label: ALL-CAPS label cards fail
tests.input:
SPEED

10x

notes: If you must list, use real hierarchy and contrast, not a grid of equal-weight cards.

title: 01 / 02 / 03 section markers
summary: A giant faint ordinal stapled to every unordered marketing section (01 Collaborate, 02 Innovate, 03 Scale) borrows costume from editorial design where an index means something; numbering is a claim of sequence, and feature sections have no order.

source.rule: Eyebrow ordinals — only genuinely numbered sections

tests.label: faint ordinal on feature section fails

notes: Number what is genuinely ordered — install steps, a changelog, a catalogue — and delete the ornamental ordinals everywhere else.

title: How-It-Works always 3 steps
summary: Round icon + number 1, 2, 3 + short text, always three steps, always the same shape: the template forces the product's real process into its shape. Present the process as it actually is — two steps or five, whatever the workflow takes.

source.rule: R-05 'How It Works' always in 3 steps

tests.label: forced three-step template fails
tests.input: Onboarding section presents exactly three numbered round-icon steps (1 Create, 2 Customize, 3 Launch) even though the product only has signup + dashboard.

tests.label: genuine two-step process passes
tests.input: Docs present the real 2-step install because that is the actual process.

notes: Three steps with round icons is fine if that is genuinely the process; otherwise use whatever shape the real workflow takes.

title: 'Trusted By' logo bar
summary: A row of generic company logos directly below the hero is a trust claim with no evidence — no real customers named, no proof of use. Show only real, verifiable logos; if there are no such customers yet, do not fabricate a logo bar.

tests.label: invented logo row fails
tests.input: Hero footer row of six gray wordmark logos for companies that never used the product, no names in the copy.

tests.label: named real customers pass
tests.input: Footer quote strip naming three real customers with permission.

notes: Real social proof beats a generic one every time; R-18 forbids inventing it.

title: 'Most Popular' middle pricing card
summary: The middle pricing tier always highlighted with a capsule badge is the default pattern, which means it is not a decision. Highlight the tier that actually serves the product's goals, or none.

tests.label: capsule badge on middle tier fails
tests.input:
Most Popular

Pro

notes: When every pricing section does it, the highlighted tier stops meaning anything.

title: 4-column template footer
summary: Product / Company / Resources / Legal columns plus a social-icon row and tiny copyright — with no variation — exist because templates have them, not because the site has that many link groups. Structure the footer around what the product actually links to.

tests.label: generic four columns fail
tests.input: Footer with Product / Company / Resources / Legal columns, social icons, copyright, on a bakery site.

tests.label: content-driven footer passes
tests.input: Single-line footer: brand + two real links + copyright, no sitemap columns.

notes: A bakery doesn't have a 'Resources' column; a single column of links can be more useful than four half-empty ones.

title: AI nav fingerprint
summary: Wordmark hard-left + 4–5 inline text links centred-or-right + CTA button hard-right + full-width + sticky + hairline border-bottom + white background is genre-blind — it lands the same on a portfolio, a bakery and a B2B SaaS. The nav should tell you what kind of site you're on.

tests.label: template nav fails
tests.input: Logo left, five centered text links (Features · Pricing · Docs · Blog · About), CTA button right, sticky with 1px bottom hairline on white.

tests.label: distinctive nav passes
tests.input: Masthead nav with the brand voice: only two destinations, aligned to the layout's grid, no hairline.

notes: Rotate among deliberate nav shapes (floating pill, newspaper masthead, terminal command, edge-aligned); reach for the template only when the page genuinely has 2 destinations.

title: Monotonous template layout
summary: Hero → subtitle → 2 CTAs → screenshot → feature grid → testimonials → FAQ → CTA → footer, in that order every time, is the training-data default rather than the product's narrative. Sections appear because the template has them; build structure around actual content needs.

source.rule: Gate 8 generic AI template / structural fingerprint

tests.label: template order fails
tests.input: Landing page ships hero, 3 features, testimonials, FAQ, final CTA, 4-col footer in the canonical order though the product has no testimonials or FAQ.

tests.label: content-driven order passes
tests.input: Page sections follow the product's real story; no section exists only because landing pages usually have it.

notes: If the product has no testimonials, there is no testimonials section. The same macrostructure repeated across outputs is the structural fingerprint of templating.

title: Uniform rhythm & one-gap spacing
summary: One spacing value (gap-4 / p-4 / space-y-4) stamped across the page, or every section the same centered-title + identical-card-grid composition, announces that nothing belongs to anything; proximity and rhythm stop carrying information. Space by relationship — tight inside groups, generous between them.

source.rule: Gate 9 sections separated only by equal whitespace

tests.label: same gap inside and between groups fails
tests.input:
Title

Body

Row

notes: The regex flags two same-value tokens near each other; the real signal is the per-file count of one token (source detection: rg -c 'space-y-4|gap-4'). A small scale with real jumps (4/8/16/32/64), used unevenly on purpose. A deliberate uniform grid (a photo wall, a calendar) is a choice.

title: Centered-everything hero
summary: min-height:100vh with the eyebrow, title, lede and CTA all stacked on the same centred vertical axis is the default LLM landing page. Pick at most two centred elements and break alignment for the rest; let the hero be the height of its content.

tests.label: 100vh centered stack fails
tests.input: .hero { min-height: 100vh; display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; } .hero * { text-align: center; }

notes: Atmospheric and playful genres may centre a hero when the canvas itself is the design; even then the eyebrow or CTA sits off-axis.

title: Default dashboard shell
summary: Left sidebar + top bar + four stat cards + a chart + a table, chosen before anyone asked what the screen is for, is the landing-page template problem in an app: swap the labels and it belongs to any product. Build the layout around the one decision the user makes on the screen.

tests.label: template shell fails
tests.input: Invoices app screen ships sidebar + topbar + 4 stat cards + donut chart + generic table without asking what the user does here.

tests.label: decision-first screen passes
tests.input: Incident screen leads with the failing jobs list and a retry action; the stat row is a footnote.

notes: If the job is 'spot the failing job and retry it', the failing jobs are the page and the stat row is a footnote.

title: Re-drawn UI chrome
summary: A fake browser bar (URL pill + traffic-light dots), fake phone frame, fake code-block window or fake IDE chrome hand-built in HTML/CSS/SVG is one of the strongest 'looks AI-generated' tells — the model invented a UI that already exists in the user's environment. Use a real screenshot in a <figure>.

tests.label: fake browser bar fails
tests.input: Hero mockup wraps a screenshot in a hand-built CSS browser frame with three colored dots and a URL pill.

tests.label: real screenshot passes
tests.input: with a hairline border at most.

notes: The page's job is to show content, not to imitate the OS; the fakery is also bad — the URL is wrong, the dots aren't macOS dots.

title: No visual identity / sterile default
summary: Swap the logo and the design still feels the same — or the page is flat white with thin grey borders, no texture, and a generic font: the 'safe' result of over-filtering without direction. A filter can remove slop; identity must be added deliberately.

source.rule: R-30 Do Not Clone Popular Products

tests.label: logo-swap test fails
tests.input: Replace the wordmark and the layout, palette and type are indistinguishable from any other SaaS template.

tests.label: distinctive result passes
tests.input: The page has a specific palette, a typeface chosen for a reason, and a composition that could belong only to this product.

notes: Identity comes from deliberate, explained choices, not from decoration. Avoid cloning Linear/Vercel/Stripe/Notion visuals unless explicitly asked.

title: transition-all / animating layout properties
summary: transition-all animates every property including ones that should be instant (visibility, focus rings), and animating width/height/margin/padding is jank on top of the decoration. Transition only the properties that carry the state change — background, border, opacity — 120–200ms, standard ease.

source.rule: 26 The springy hover (transition-all is the tell inside the tell)

notes: Specify the properties; hover feedback is a surface shift, not growth.

title: Springy hover / overshoot easing
summary: hover:scale-105 and translate-y lift across every card, plus bouncy cubic-bezier overshoots on buttons/modals/tooltips, are a tasteless throwback; scaling a card on hover says nothing. Hover feedback is a surface shift (background, border, opacity); reserve springs for things that genuinely move through space.

source.rule: Gate 12 bouncy/overshoot easings on UI state
R-19 Animations (Fade Up + Floating + Scale + Bounce)

notes: Pick one signal per element — a 1px translate, a colour shift, or an underline thickening — never all four at once; reserve overshoots for genuine physical interactions (drag-and-drop release).

title: Wobbling spinner
summary: A loading spinner whose arc doesn't rotate around its own centre wobbles because the spin keyframe replaces the whole transform, clobbering the centering translate(-50%,-50%) — the most-watched element on the page limping at the worst moment, an admission nobody watched the interface move. Give the rotation a real centre; then watch one full revolution.

tests.label: keyframe clobbers centering fails
tests.input: @keyframes spin { to { transform: rotate(360deg); } } .spinner { transform: translate(-50%, -50%); animation: spin 1s linear infinite; }

tests.label: rotate on standalone property passes
tests.input: .spinner { position: absolute; inset: 50% auto auto 50%; translate: -50% -50%; rotate: 0deg; animation: spin 1s linear infinite; }

notes: Centre the artwork in its own box, keep centering out of the animated transform (wrapper or the standalone rotate property), and watch one full revolution — code tells never replace the visual check.

title: Endless pulses and loops
summary: Elements that pulse, bounce or float forever with no user trigger are noise — perpetual motion competes with the content and never stops. Motion must have a clear UX purpose; animation guides attention to a moment, it does not run on a loop.

source.rule: R-19 Animations — endless pulses and loops

tests.label: pulsing stat card fails
tests.input:
Loading totals…
forever on a static page

tests.label: finite spinner passes
tests.input: .spinner { animation: spin 1s linear infinite; } — a loading indicator whose loop is its function

notes: A genuine loading spinner is the legitimate infinite loop; if the MOTION dial is 1 (hover states only), an endless loop is a FAIL against the declared dial.

title: Animate-on-scroll on everything
summary: Every section fades in, every list staggers, the page never settles — a page where everything animates has no focal point. Pick one orchestrated entrance; let the rest just be there. Motion must match the declared MOTION dial.

tests.label: scroll-reveal on every section fails
tests.input: Every section and list item has data-aos='fade-up' with stagger delays; the page never settles.

tests.label: one hero entrance passes
tests.input: A single orchestrated hero entrance; all other sections render statically.

notes: Not everything moves: the hero speaks, the supporting elements stay calm. A claimed 'cinematic' page must actually move; a claimed 'static' page must not.

title: Missing prefers-reduced-motion fallback
summary: Every transform/animation keyframe needs a @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) fallback — motion without one is an accessibility defect and ships as slop to vestibular-sensitive users.

source.rule: Gate 27 reduced-motion fallback for every keyframe

tests.label: uncovered keyframes fail
tests.input: @keyframes float {…} with no prefers-reduced-motion media query anywhere in the file.

notes: Also avoid content that flashes more than 3 times per second (photosensitive epilepsy).

title: Transition duration outside 0.2–0.3s
summary: Smooth transitions on state changes run 0.2–0.3 seconds with an ease curve; faster than 0.15s feels jarring, slower than 0.4s feels laggy, no transition feels broken.
notes: Per-property durations are fine; the tell is a duration outside the band on a UI state change.

title: Emoji everywhere
summary: An emoji on every heading, button and bullet (🚀 launch, ⚡ fast, 🔒 secure) is borrowed warmth standing in for tone that copy and design should carry. Cut decorative emoji from the UI; keep one only where it genuinely carries information, like a real status.

source.rule: Gate 30b emoji glyph as feature/step/pricing icon
Rule 2 Emoji — functional or brand-driven only

notes: False positives: emoji inside a documented code sample, an emoji-picker feature, user-generated content; a functional status emoji may be defended but still triggers the range. Regex needs the u flag for \u{...} ranges.

title: Generic AI icons
summary: Sparkle, star, magic, lightning, diamond, cube, robot and AI-orb glyphs are the generic vocabulary of 'AI product' — they communicate nothing about the specific feature. Icons must be genuinely relevant to the content; if no appropriate icon exists, use none.
notes: False positives: a magic-wand action inside a real editing tool. The feature label does the work; relevance should be writable in one line.

title: Arrow on every button
summary: → / ↗ placed on almost every button as pure decoration turns the arrow into a pattern, not a signal. Keep direction cues for the action that genuinely benefits from one, sized proportionally, with the purpose written down.
notes: Arrows are not the default identity for buttons; not every CTA needs one.

title: Aurora blobs / floating orbs / decoration without purpose
summary: Flowing mesh or conic gradients in purple-to-pink, blurred coloured circles drifting behind the hero, and random ornaments ('42' in a corner, a cursor with no command) are generic ambience with no semantic anchor — 'I needed something here, so I added something here'. Decoration must be motivated: a cursor inside a typed command, a numeral that names an issue or year, a gradient that responds to interaction.

source.rule: Aurora-blob background / Floating-orb decoration / Cursor follower dots

notes: The hero doesn't need depth; it needs a strong typographic anchor. A deliberate two-stop gradient + feTurbulence grain at <0.1 opacity is the acceptable 'atmosphere' recipe.

title: Stock / AI illustrations
summary: Undraw/Storyset downloads, smooth mesh-blob characters, and 'AI-style' SVG people with identical posing fill space without serving the content — the audience pattern-matches them as AI in milliseconds. Illustrations must have a direct connection to the product; otherwise use real screenshots, or none.

source.rule: Rule 4 Imagery — real, licensed, or honest placeholder

tests.label: stock blob illustration fails
tests.input: Hero features an undraw.co 3D blob character with a laptop, unrelated to the logistics product being sold.

tests.label: real screenshot passes
tests.input: Feature section uses an honest product screenshot instead of decoration.

notes: An honest placeholder — striped background with a monospace label like 'product shot (1200×800)' — beats a bad illustration: it signals 'asset needed' without pretending to be final. Skeleton-block previews used as the product shot are the same tell.

title: Mismatched icon sets
summary: Material Icons in the navbar, Heroicons in the feature cards, Lucide in the footer and an emoji in a hero badge mixes three stroke voices — icons are typography, and you wouldn't ship three body fonts. Pick one icon library per project and hold it.

params.note: flag when >1 distinct library import in one project

source.rule: Gate 30a mixing two or more icon libraries

tests.label: three libraries on one page fail
tests.input: import { Settings } from "lucide-react"; import { Cog } from "@heroicons/react"; import SettingsIcon from "@mui/icons-material/Settings";

notes: Lucide is the default for SaaS, Phosphor when you need weight variants, Heroicons for Tailwind/shadcn projects — pick one per project.

title: Animation-tech shortcuts (Lottie / Three.js for a still job)
summary: Reaching for a LottieFiles community animation (spinner, checkmark draw) when CSS or hand-built SVG would do it in zero bytes, or a WebGL hero the user can't touch — 100–300 KB of Three.js for a thing that could be a static photograph — is a shortcut the audience reads as one. Lottie is Tier F, last resort; Three.js must earn its place by being interactive.

source.rule: Gate 31 Lottie is last resort, not the default
Lottie shortcut / Three.js for a still object

tests.label: CSS spinner passes
tests.input: .spinner { border: 2px solid; border-top-color: transparent; border-radius: 50%; animation: spin 0.8s linear infinite; }

notes: Spinning logo → CSS keyframes; checkmark → SVG stroke-dasharray; loading dots → CSS animation-delay. If the user can't manipulate the 3D, it doesn't justify Three.js.

title: AI copywriting voice & banned openings
summary: 'It's not just X — it's Y', 'Say goodbye to X', three-word triads, and opening lines like 'Built for the modern team', 'Unleash your [X]', 'Where X meets Y', 'Supercharge your workflow' are the rhythmic fingerprint of generated copy — symmetrical, one notch too excited, specifics-free. Write something specific: real numbers, nouns, consequences.

matcher.pattern: not just .{1,40}\bit'?s\b|say goodbye to|meet your new|supercharge|unlock the power|in seconds, not|\b(blazing[- ]fast|effortless|seamless|game[- ]changer|next[- ]level)\b|\b(growth|security|process|privacy|productivity|compliance|feature|innovation) theater\b|built for the modern (team|age)|unleash your|where [a-z]+ meets|empower (your|every)|reimagine the way|innovative solutions|seamless integration|in today'?s digital|next-?generation|revolutionary|cutting[- ]edge|ai[- ]powered

tests.label: template voice fails
tests.input: It's not just a CRM — it's your revenue copilot. Say goodbye to spreadsheets forever.

tests.label: specific copy passes
tests.input: Track every deal from first touch to signature, with deadlines that follow the actual close date.

notes: False positives: a genuine quote, or a doc that discusses these phrases. 'We killed the X theater' framing is the same tic — say plainly what the thing does or doesn't do.

title: Generic CTAs
summary: 'Get Started', 'Learn More', 'Try Now', 'Explore', 'Discover' as default CTAs are specific to nothing; CTAs must name the product context and the intended action ('Start Your Free Trial', 'Watch Live Demo', 'Create Free Account'). Use the verb for the action the button performs.

source.rule: Buttons — use the verb for the action
Chapter 12 one clear CTA / specific verbs

notes: 'Continue' is acceptable only as the secondary button of a multi-step flow. A screen has one primary action; multiple competing CTAs dilute every action.

title: Microcopy bans (click here / oops / filler)
summary: 'Click here', 'Oops!', 'Uh oh!', 'Something went wrong', 'Enter your email below' are empty or perform embarrassment for the user's input; errors are instructions — what broke, why, how to fix — and link text must stand alone. No exclamation marks in error states, no humour in frustration paths.

matcher.pattern: >\s*Click here\s*<|oops!|uh oh!|something went wrong|enter your (email|password) below|invalid input|error occurred

source.rule: Chapter 11 form feedback / errors name the thing

tests.label: instructional error passes
tests.input: That card was declined. Try another card, or contact your bank.

notes: Link text must stand alone ('View pricing plans' beats 'Click here'); if the input is below, you don't need to say so.

title: Placeholder names & startup clichés
summary: 'Jane Doe', 'John Smith', 'Acme', 'Nexus', 'Lorem Ipsum' and the startup-cliché vocabulary (Seamless, Unleash, Elevate, Empower, Delight, Magical) are stock filler that marks the page as generated — name real people and real things.

tests.label: stock testimonial name fails
tests.input: "Jane Doe, Head of Growth at Acme"

tests.label: real attribution passes
tests.input: "Priya Nair, VP Engineering at Northwind Logistics"

notes: Lorem Ipsum is allowed only on a lorem-ipsum tool; 'Acme' on a demo page is fine only as an explicitly labeled placeholder.

title: Empty states without a next action
summary: 'No data available' with an illustration or a bare spinner tells the user nothing — no cause, no next action, no idea whether this is normal. An empty state names what's empty, why it matters, and the one action that fills it.

source.rule: Empty states — three beats (name, why, one button)

tests.label: dead empty state fails
tests.input: Empty inbox screen shows 'No data available' next to a decorative illustration and nothing else.

tests.label: actionable empty state passes
tests.input: 'No projects yet. Projects group your tasks and team.' + Create project button.

notes: First run, filtered-to-nothing, and permission-denied are different screens and should read differently.

title: Invented stat row / fake metrics
summary: Three big round numbers — 10k+ developers, 99.9% uptime, 24/7 support — on a product that launched yesterday are social proof turned into a layout, filled whether or not the proof exists; one invented figure poisons every true one beside it. Show a number only if you measured it and say where it came from.

source.rule: R-17 Data & Numbers (no source = no numbers)

tests.label: odd sourced figure passes
tests.input: 1,847 CI runs yesterday, down from 2,031 the week before

notes: A stat is also never the hero's sole headline. Real numbers are odd and specific; fix by replacing with '—' and a labelled grey block, asking the user for the figure, or rebuilding the section without the proof slot. Also covers dashboard stat cards with invented deltas ('+12% this week').

title: Fake testimonials & invented people
summary: AI avatars, random names and job titles, fictional reviews — and the dashboard variant, a filler activity feed of invented people and events ('Sarah Chen updated a document, 2 hours ago') — are fabricated social proof; a page that lies on its proof bar can't be trusted on its claims. No real testimonials → no testimonials section.

source.rule: R-38 Real Content or Honest Placeholder

tests.label: invented quote fails
tests.input: Testimonial section ships five quotes from made-up people with AI-generated avatar photos and no source.

tests.label: sourced quote passes
tests.input: One quote from a named customer with permission, linked to their public profile.

notes: An honest empty state beats a fabricated feed. Real social proof must be verifiable (R-18, C-5).

title: Fabricated trust & compliance claims
summary: Inventing security, compliance or performance claims — 'SOC 2 compliant', 'ISO 27001', 'Enterprise-grade security', '300% faster' — for a product with no such evidence is a Hard Gate failure. If there is no real data, show no claim.

tests.label: unbacked compliance badge fails
tests.input: Hero badge claims 'SOC 2 compliant' with no audit, no report, no evidence.

tests.label: specific real capability passes
tests.input: Data is encrypted in transit with TLS 1.3; backups are stored in EU regions.

notes: Same family as fake statistics and fake testimonials — evidence over claims (C-5): anything presented as fact is real and verifiable, or it is not shown at all.

title: Assumed logos, avatars & profile photos
summary: Creating app logos, avatars, profile photos, or a 'Trusted By' logo row without explicit instructions — purely on assumption — is fabricating assets as if final; use clear placeholders ([LOGO], initial-based avatar, 'Coming soon') and never disguise them as final.

source.rule: R-38 Real Content or Honest Placeholder

tests.label: invented logo fails
tests.input: Product ships a designed logo mark, six customer logos and three team avatars the model invented because the brief didn't provide them.

tests.label: honest placeholder passes
tests.input: Header uses the product name in a clean typeface plus a [LOGO] marker pending the real asset.

notes: If asking is not possible, placeholders must be visible as placeholders: logo → text or [LOGO]; profile photo → initial-based avatar; statistics → not displayed or marked [REAL DATA].

title: Dead interactive elements (nav links & controls to nowhere)
summary: Navbar links to pages or sections that do not exist, buttons that do nothing, dropdowns that won't open, forms that can't submit — the visual is finished but the behavior is not. Every interactive element has a real destination/behavior, or it is removed; if a feature isn't built, leave it out or label it 'Coming soon'.

source.rule: R-26 Interactive Elements (real behavior or removed)

tests.label: dead nav fails
tests.input: Navbar lists Features, Pricing, About — none of which exist as sections or pages on the site.

tests.label: real destinations pass
tests.input: Every nav item has a real href to an existing section; a not-yet-built feature is labelled 'Coming soon'.

notes: A placeholder is acceptable only with a clear // TODO comment AND a visible label to the user (e.g. 'Coming soon'); a link or button must scroll to an existing section, open a real modal (Escape-closable), or perform a real action.

title: Irrelevant FAQ
summary: An FAQ of template questions ('Is my data secure?', 'Can I cancel anytime?') with no real relevance to the product does more damage to trust than having no FAQ at all. Every question must address a real concern of that product's users, or the section doesn't ship.

tests.label: generic FAQ fails
tests.input: A chat-widget startup ships an FAQ with 'Is my data secure?' and 'Can I cancel anytime?' — questions no user of this product asks.

tests.label: specific FAQ passes
tests.input: FAQ answers 'Which model runs the summarizer?' and 'How are transcripts stored?' — the questions this product's users actually ask.

notes: If you do not know what questions are actually asked, do not create an FAQ section.

title: Premium-consumer warm-craft palette (beige+brass+espresso)
summary: For premium-consumer briefs (cookware, wellness, artisan, luxury, DTC home goods) the LLM default is warm beige/cream backgrounds, brass/clay/oxblood/ochre accents, and espresso near-black text — the same hex families on every generated site, making the brand invisible. The beige+brass+espresso family is banned as the default reach; it is acceptable only when the brand brief names those colors or the brand is genuinely vintage/artisan with a documented palette.
notes: ZS-UI-003 covers the Tailwind amber/stone warm ramp; this targets the exact hex families above. Palette-rotation rule: do not ship the same warm-craft family twice in a row across projects.

title: Eyebrow rationing: max 1 per 3 sections
summary: An 'eyebrow' — the small uppercase wide-tracked label above a section headline (text-[11px] uppercase tracking-[0.18em]) — appears above EVERY section on AI-built sites, producing the same templated rhythm. Hard rule: maximum 1 eyebrow per 3 sections (hero counts as 1); if section A has one, the next two cannot.

source.rule: EYEBROW RESTRAINT (mandatory, the #1 violated rule in production tests)

tests.label: eyebrow on every section fails
tests.input: A 9-section page with an `uppercase tracking-[0.18em]` label above all nine headlines — count 9 > ceil(9/3).

tests.label: rationed eyebrows pass
tests.input: A 9-section page with exactly 3 `uppercase tracking` eyebrows, spaced one per three sections.

notes: Hero counts as one section. Section location on the page already categorizes; the headline alone is enough — when in doubt, drop the eyebrow entirely.

title: Hero budget: headline ≤2 lines, subtext ≤20 words / ≤4 lines, top padding ≤pt-24
summary: The hero must fit in the initial viewport: headline max 2 lines at desktop, subtext max 20 words AND max 4 lines, CTAs visible without scroll, and hero top padding max pt-24 (~6rem). A 4-line hero headline is a font-size error, never a copy-length error; if the value-prop cannot be said in 20 words, the value-prop is unclear.

source.rule: Hero MUST fit in the initial viewport (Headline max 2 lines, subtext max 20 words AND max 3-4 lines)

tests.label: oversized hero fails
tests.input: Hero at text-7xl: the headline wraps to 4 lines, the subtext runs 41 words across 6 lines, and pt-32 floats the CTA below the fold.

tests.label: budgeted hero passes
tests.input: Hero at text-5xl: headline fits 2 lines, subtext is 18 words across 3 lines, pt-16 keeps the CTA above the fold.

notes: Also enforces hero stack discipline: max 4 text elements (eyebrow OR brand strip, headline, subtext, CTAs) — no tagline below the CTAs, no trust micro-strip, no pricing teaser, no feature bullets, no avatar row inside the hero; those move to dedicated sections below.

title: Duplicate CTA intent
summary: Two CTAs with the same intent on one page is a Pre-Flight Fail: 'Get in touch' + 'Contact us' + 'Let's talk' are all contact intent; 'Try free' + 'Get started' + 'Sign up free' are all signup intent. Pick ONE label per intent and use it everywhere (nav, hero, footer).

tests.label: same intent multiple labels fails
tests.input: Nav says 'Get in touch', the hero says 'Contact us', the footer says 'Let's talk' — three labels, one contact intent.

tests.label: one label per intent passes
tests.input: 'Start a project' is the single contact CTA in nav, hero, and footer; a separate 'See selected work' links to the portfolio.

title: Section layout repetition (≥4 families per 8 sections; zigzag cap 2)
summary: A layout family (3-column image cards, full-width quote, split image+text) may appear at most ONCE per page; a landing page with 8 sections must use at least 4 different families. Consecutive left/right image+text zigzag alternation is capped at 2 — the 3rd consecutive image+text split is a Pre-Flight Fail.

tests.label: repeated families fail
tests.input: An 8-section page built from 2 families: five 3-column image-card grids plus three consecutive image+text split rows alternating left and right.

tests.label: diverse families pass
tests.input: 8 sections using 4 families: one split, one bento, one full-width quote, one stats band — and never 3 image+text splits in a row.

title: Bento grid cell-count mismatch (N items must fill N cells)
summary: A bento grid has exactly as many cells as content items: 3 items → 3 cells, 5 items → 5 cells (2+3, 3+2, hero+4...). An empty tile in the middle or at the end means the grid was planned wrong — reshape the grid, never paste a blank tile.

tests.label: empty bento cell fails
tests.input: A 6-cell bento grid with only 4 real cards and one empty white tile at the end.

tests.label: exact cell count passes
tests.input: 5 content items fill exactly 5 cells in a 2+3 bento split.

notes: Companion to ZS-UI-045 (monotonous template layout): this is the mechanical cell-count check.

title: Split-header / floating sub-text section heads
summary: The split-header pattern — big headline in a left col-span-7/8 with a small explainer paragraph floating in a right col-span-4/5 — is banned as default; sections should have ONE focused message, stacked vertically (headline on top, body ≤65ch below). A tiny corner paragraph with no alignment to anything is the same tell.

source.rule: NO floating top-right sub-text in section headings

tests.label: floating explainer fails
tests.input: Section header: left col-span-8 headline, right col-span-4 explainer paragraph floating with no alignment to anything else in the column.

tests.label: stacked header passes
tests.input: Headline on top, 65ch body paragraph stacked directly below it.

notes: Reach for the split only with a real compositional reason — the right column carrying a visual or interactive element, not filler text. Related to ZS-UI-020 (eyebrow-left variant of the same column-split device).

title: Navigation single-line ≤80px at desktop
summary: Navigation must render on a single line at desktop (lg 1024px) and cap at 80px height (default 64-72px). A two-line nav or a giant 'agency' bar eating 15% of the viewport is broken design — condense labels, drop secondary items, or move to a hamburger.

source.rule: Navigation MUST render on a single line on desktop
Navigation height cap: 80px max desktop, default 64-72px

tests.label: oversized nav fails
tests.input: A 96px nav with logo, 7 links, a CTA and a phone number wrapping to a second line at lg.

tests.label: compact nav passes
tests.input: A 64px single-line nav; secondary items collapse into a hamburger below 1024px.

title: Scroll cues
summary: Scroll cues — 'Scroll', '↓ scroll', 'Scroll to explore', animated mouse-wheel icons, bouncing chevrons — label the obvious: users at the top of a page know what scroll is. The bottom of the viewport does not need a caption.

matcher.pattern: (?:Scroll to (?:explore|walk through|discover|learn)|Scroll down|scroll to explore|Swipe (?:down|up)|scroll indicator|mouse-wheel)

source.rule: No Filler Text: 'Scroll to explore', 'Swipe down', scroll arrow icons, bouncing chevrons are BANNED

tests.label: scroll cue fails
tests.input: ↓ Scroll to explore

notes: A plain arrow glyph is acceptable; a section-numbered 'Scroll · 001 Capabilities' cue is the same tell with an ordinal bolted on.

title: Decorative status dots on nav / list rows
summary: A plain colored dot before every nav link, list row, badge, or status label is decoration with no signal — the visual of 'status' without any status. Dots are acceptable only when they convey real semantic state (live server status, availability flag) and are used sparingly — one per page section max.

source.rule: NO decorative colored status dots on every list/nav/badge
ZERO decorative status dots by default

tests.label: dots on nav rows fail
tests.input: WorkAbout

tests.label: real status dot passes
tests.input: All systems operational

notes: ZS-UI-037 covers the glowing/pulsing halo variant; this covers plain decorative dots. A dot without a label word next to it is decoration, not status — the emerald-hue dot with a real label is the allowed form.

title: Locale / time / weather strips
summary: Locale, city, time, and weather strips ('LIS 14:23 · 18°C', 'Lisbon, working with founders', '1200-690 Lisbon, Portugal' as atmosphere) in headers, heroes, or footers are agency-portfolio decoration for 99% of briefs. Allowed only for genuinely place-distributed studios, travel brands, or real venues; a single contact address in the footer is fine.

source.rule: Locale / city-name / time / weather strips are banned for 99% of briefs

title: Version stamps & build footers
summary: Version stamps ('V0.6', 'BETA', 'INVITE-ONLY PREVIEW', 'EARLY ACCESS') as hero eyebrows, and version footers ('v1.4.2', 'Build 0048', 'last sync 4s ago · main') on marketing/landing/portfolio pages, are CLI/devtool fixtures, not landing-page content — they scream generated.

source.rule: NO version labels in the hero
NO version footers on marketing pages

notes: Exempt when the brief is explicitly a product launch/preview (a real beta program) or a devtool/docs site where build info is real content.

title: Div-based fake screenshots
summary: A 'product preview' hand-built from styled <div> rectangles — fake browser chrome with traffic-light dots, a fake task list, a fake terminal, a fake dashboard — is the #1 LLM-design tell. If you need to show a product, use a real screenshot, a generated image, a real component preview, or none at all.

source.rule: NO div-based fake product UI in the hero

tests.label: div mock fails
tests.input: Hero shows a 'product preview' assembled from styled divs: three dots for browser chrome, a fake task list, and a fake terminal window — no real screenshot anywhere.

tests.label: real screenshot passes
tests.input: Hero shows the product UI as a real screenshot with next/image priority, or a genuine interactive component preview.

title: AI-invented spec precision
summary: Numbers with fake engineering precision — '5.8 mm case', '13.4 lb', '4.1× faster', '0.6 ctx-switches/day' — invent a spec aesthetic the brand never measured. Precision figures must come from real data (brief, brand guidelines, public metrics) or be explicitly labeled mock.

tests.label: invented spec fails
tests.input: Hero spec strip: '5.8 mm case · 13.4 lb · 4.1× faster' — precision the brand never claimed.

tests.label: no invented decimals passes
tests.input: The spec sheet lists '10-year warranty' and 'hand-polished brass', with no invented decimals.

notes: Complements ZS-UI-070 (invented stat rows): 070 targets dashboard stat rows and round social-proof figures; this targets decimal-precision measurements on consumer/spec content.

title: Generic step labels
summary: Generic progression labels — 'Step 1 / Step 2 / Step 3', 'Stage 1', 'Phase 01', 'Pass One' — label the container, not the content. The actual step content is the label; use the verb-noun directly ('Install', 'Configure', 'Ship').
notes: ZS-UI-040 covers the always-3-steps template; this covers the ordinal label itself.

title: Poetic / performative section labels
summary: Poetic, performative-craftsman labels — 'From the field', 'Field notes', 'On our desks', 'Loose plates', 'Currently on the bench' — on quote, blog, or sidebar sections read as fake authenticity. Use plain functional labels ('Testimonials', 'Latest writing', 'Now working on') or skip the label.

source.rule: NO 'From the field' / 'Field notes' / 'Currently on the bench' / 'On our desks' / 'Loose plates' style poetic labels
NO 'Quietly in use at' / 'Quietly trusted by' social-proof headers

title: LLM-favorite display serifs (Fraunces / Instrument Serif)
summary: Fraunces and Instrument Serif are the two LLM-favorite display serifs — they appear in nearly every generated 'editorial' hero and are now themselves convergence tells. Use them only with explicit brand justification, or rotate from a broader pool (PP Editorial New, GT Sectra, Recoleta, Canela, Cormorant...).

source.rule: Specifically BANNED as defaults: Fraunces and Instrument_Serif (the two LLM-favorite display serifs)
Use only with clear intent (now themselves tells): Space Grotesk, Geist, Instrument Serif

notes: Space Grotesk and Geist are already banned as defaults by ZS-UI-015; this closes the display-serif gap. Purpose-gate: a brand brief that literally names these faces is exempt.

title: Accent hue in the AI band (OKLCH H 250–320)
summary: OKLCH hue ~250-320 — indigo, violet, purple — is the reddest ocean in AI UI: the literal default accent band. Unless the brief demands it, pick an uncontested hue (orange, brick, crimson, grass, teal, amber) for the accent. A brand that genuinely IS purple is exempt.

source.rule: Avoid OKLCH hue ~250 to 320 for accents unless the brief demands it
THE LILA RULE: the AI Purple/Blue glow aesthetic is discouraged as a default

notes: Distinct from ZS-UI-001 (indigo→violet gradient) and ZS-UI-004 (stock semantic status palette): this is the accent-hue band rule. LILA override: a brand that is genuinely purple stays purple — execute with intent, not gradient slop.

title: Gray text on colored backgrounds
summary: Gray text dropped onto a colored/tinted surface was never toned to its background — the safest AI move and a readability failure. On colored backgrounds use the same hue, darker and desaturated, never gray.

source.rule: No gray text on colored backgrounds. Use the same hue, darker and desaturated
On colored backgrounds use the same hue darker and desaturated, never gray

notes: ZS-UI-003 already catches gray-400/500 on a few warm tints; this is the generalized rule for any gray step on any colored surface, plus the CSS color/background form.

title: Blob-rounding on small cards (radius >16px)
summary: Small cards are capped at ~16px radius; rounded-3xl (24px) and above on small cards is 'blob-rounding' — blob geometry that reads as generic. Radius above 16px belongs to hero imagery and large panels, not to small cards.

source.rule: Radius <= 16px on small cards. No blob-rounding (24px+)

notes: Distinct from ZS-UI-032 (pill-everything, uniform max radius across element kinds): this caps small-card radius specifically. Avatars and genuine pills are exempt.

title: Hairline border + wide diffuse shadow on the same element
summary: A hairline border AND a wide diffuse shadow on the same element commits to two separators doing one job. Pick one: a defined edge or a soft elevation — never both.

source.rule: hairline border and diffuse drop shadow stacked on the same element
No hairline border AND wide diffuse shadow on the same element. Commit to one: a defined edge or a soft elevation

notes: ZS-UI-033 mentions the 'ghost card' variant in its notes; this is the dedicated rule with its own matcher.

title: Canonical AI-authored easing curves
summary: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) and cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) are the two 'authored' curves documented in the standard motion references and now recur in nearly every generated stylesheet — they have become the new default. Pick a curve from the wider documented range (Material, Carbon, iOS sheet) or author your own.

source.rule: Useful authored curves: a strong ease-out cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1), a strong ease-in-out cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)

notes: The fingerprint shifts: a curve documented as the standard authored default in every motion reference becomes the statistical median of generated UI. Purpose-gate: using them via a documented token is a choice; defaulting to them is the tell.

title: Animating from scale(0)
summary: Nothing in the real world appears from nothing: elements animating from scale(0) look like they materialize out of nowhere. Start from scale(0.9-0.97) combined with opacity so the element already has a shape and grows into place.

source.rule: Never animate from scale(0). Start from about 0.9 to 0.97 so the element already has a shape

title: Dark-mode elevation via lightness, not shadows (base 8–12% L)
summary: Dark mode is not an inversion: pure-black backgrounds vibrate, shadows barely register, and saturated accents glare. Base the darkest surface at 8-12% lightness (Material's #121212 is the reference), express elevation by making raised surfaces LIGHTER (cards ~L14-16, popovers ~L18-20) — never with drop shadows — and keep body text off-white.

source.rule: Backgrounds: never pure black... A common base sits around 8 to 12 percent lightness
Pure #000000 background. Replace with off-black, dark charcoal, or tinted dark (#0a0a0a, #121212, or a dark navy)

tests.label: shadowed dark surfaces fail
tests.input: Dark mode: base #000000, every card the same #121212 separated only by a drop shadow, pure #FFF body text.

tests.label: lightness ramp passes
tests.input: Dark mode: base #121212, cards #1a1a1a, popovers #222; elevation by lightness, off-white #EDEDED text.

notes: ZS-UI-007 covers the literal pure #000/#FFF regex; this is the elevation model — the closer a surface is to the user, the lighter it is, and drop shadows do not read on dark.

title: Default icon library tell (Lucide / Heroicons / Feather)
summary: Lucide (the shadcn default), Heroicons, and Feather are baked into starter kits and generated components — they signal 'generic template' even though they are well made. The unmodified default set defining the look is the tell; switch sets (Phosphor, Tabler, Iconoir, Hugeicons) or at minimum customize stroke width and corner radius.

source.rule: Lucide is the shadcn default and is now baked into countless templates and generated components, so it signals 'generic template' even though it is well made
Lucide or Feather icons exclusively. These are the 'default' AI icon choice

notes: ZS-UI-063 flags mixing sets; this flags defaulting to the starter-kit set alone. Customizing stroke/radius of the default set is an acceptable escape.

title: ease-in on UI transitions
summary: ease-in starts slow and speeds up — it delays the exact moment the user is watching, so a dropdown at 300ms ease-in feels slower than the same duration ease-out. Never use ease-in for UI animations; reserve it for exit-to-nowhere.

source.rule: Never use ease-in for UI animations
ease-in for exit only... never for things the user is waiting on (it speeds up at the end and feels laggy)

notes: ease-in-out is not flagged; the ban is the plain ease-in keyword on enter/state-change transitions.

title: Popover / menu transform-origin
summary: A popover, menu, or dropdown should scale from its trigger, not from its own center — center-origin scaling on a corner-anchored menu is a tell. Wire the origin to the trigger position (Radix/Base UI expose --transform-origin). Modals are the exception: they stay centered.

source.rule: A popover or menu should scale from its trigger, not from its own center; wire the origin to the trigger position

notes: Modals keep transform-origin center — they are not anchored to a trigger.

title: Hover states gated behind @media (hover:hover) (pointer:fine)
summary: Touch devices fire hover on tap, causing false positives: gate hover-triggered animation behind `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` so touch users never get a phantom hover state.

tests.label: ungated hover fails
tests.input: Card hover lifts with translate-y and scale, with no `@media (hover: hover)` gate — the hover fires on every tap on a touch device.

tests.label: gated hover passes
tests.input: The hover lift sits inside `@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)`; base styles are unchanged on touch.

title: Keyboard-initiated actions never animated
summary: Animation on high-frequency, keyboard-initiated actions — a command palette toggled with ⌘K, menu navigation — is friction: it makes a power user's repeated action feel slow and disconnected. Frequency gates animation: 100+ times/day → no animation, ever; occasional (modals, toasts) → standard animation.

source.rule: do not animate frequent, utilitarian ones

tests.label: animated palette fails
tests.input: Opening the command palette via ⌘K — used a hundred times a day — plays a 400ms scale-and-fade every single time.

tests.label: instant palette passes
tests.input: The command palette appears instantly with no open animation; only first-time onboarding uses motion.

title: Transition duration by element size
summary: Duration scales with the element's size and travel: button press 100-160ms, tooltips/small popovers 125-200ms, dropdowns/selects 150-250ms, modals/drawers 200-500ms — and most UI stays under 300ms. A 450ms dropdown feels sluggish next to an 180ms one.

source.rule: Duration table: Button press 100-160ms, Tooltips 125-200ms, Dropdowns 150-250ms, Modals 200-500ms; UI animations should stay under 300ms
Most UI animations should stay under 300ms. Micro feedback 100-150ms; standard transitions 150-250ms; larger surfaces 250-500ms

notes: Refines ZS-UI-057 (generic 0.2-0.3s band): sheets and drawers may legitimately run to 500ms with an iOS-like curve; a 450ms dropdown cannot.

title: Generic card boundary (1px gray border / harsh dark shadow)
summary: The generic AI card look: a 1px solid gray border (gray-200/#e5e7eb family) or a harsh dark drop shadow (Tailwind shadow-md, rgba(0,0,0,0.3)) as the universal card boundary. Prefer a defined edge, tinted low-alpha shadows tight to the surface, or spacing alone.

source.rule: Banned Borders & Shadows: Generic 1px solid gray borders. Harsh, dark drop shadows (shadow-md, rgba(0,0,0,0.3))
Generic card look (border + shadow + white background)

notes: Purpose-gate: a hairline border is fine when it separates genuinely distinct content; the tell is it as the universal card boundary. ZS-UI-033 covers oversized 60px+ blur shadows; this covers the harsh default band (shadow-md / 30% black).

title: h-screen / 100vh full-height sections
summary: height: 100vh / h-screen for full-height sections causes catastrophic layout jumping on mobile browsers (the iOS Safari address-bar viewport bug). Always use min-h-[100dvh] so the section grows with the dynamic viewport.

source.rule: NEVER use h-screen for full-height Hero sections. ALWAYS use min-h-[100dvh]
Never use h-screen for full-height sections — always use min-h-[100dvh] to prevent iOS Safari viewport jumping
Full-height sections must use min-h-[100dvh] — never h-screen (iOS Safari catastrophic jump)

title: Arbitrary z-index (z-50 / z-[9999])
summary: Arbitrary z-index values (z-50, z-[9999], z-index: 9999) sprinkle magic numbers through components until a modal fights a toast. Use z-index strictly for systemic layer contexts (sticky nav, modals, overlays, tooltips) and document the scale in a constants file.

source.rule: Do not use arbitrary z-50 or z-[9999]
Z-Index Restraint: NEVER spam arbitrary z-50 or z-10
Arbitrary z-index values like 9999. Establish a clean z-index scale in the theme/variables

title: Symmetric vertical padding without optical adjustment
summary: Top and bottom padding that are always identical (py-24, padding: 6rem 0 on every section) read as mechanical; adjust optically — the bottom padding often needs to be slightly larger because a page's visual weight settles downward.

source.rule: Symmetrical vertical padding. Top and bottom padding are always identical. Adjust optically — bottom padding often needs to be slightly larger

notes: The Tailwind variant — the same py-N utility on every section — is the same tell; check by counting identical py-* values across sections.

title: Random dark section in a light page
summary: A single dark-background section breaking an otherwise light page (or vice versa) reads as a copy-paste accident. Either commit to a full dark mode or keep one background tone throughout; for contrast, use a slightly darker shade of the same palette, not a sudden jump to #111.

source.rule: Random dark sections in a light mode page (or vice versa)
Page Theme Lock (Light / Dark Mode Consistency)

tests.label: stray dark band fails
tests.input: A light #f7f5f1 page with one `bg-[#111]` CTA band in the middle — the dark section reads as an accident.

tests.label: consistent theme passes
tests.input: The page stays light throughout; the CTA band uses a slightly darker shade of the page's own cream.

title: Rocketship-for-Launch / shield-for-Security cliché icons
summary: The cliché metaphor icons — a rocketship for 'Launch', a shield for 'Security' — are the default AI icon choice. Replace clichés with less obvious metaphors (bolt, fingerprint, spark, vault) that actually match the feature.

source.rule: Rocketship for 'Launch', shield for 'Security'. Replace cliche metaphors with less obvious icons (bolt, fingerprint, spark, vault)

notes: Related to ZS-UI-059 (generic AI glyphs): 059 covers sparkle/star/zap glyphs; this covers the metaphor clichés.

title: Missing favicon
summary: Shipping without a favicon leaves a default globe in the tab and a blank bookmark — a finish-gate failure that reads as unfinished. Always include a branded favicon (SVG or ICO) referenced from the document head.

source.rule: Missing favicon. Always include a branded favicon.

tests.label: no favicon fails
tests.input: The app ships with no `<link rel="icon">` — the browser tab shows the default globe and the bookmark has no icon.

tests.label: favicon present passes
tests.input: <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" /> renders a branded mark in the tab.

title: Fake system-metric sections & 'LABEL // YEAR' stamps
summary: 'SYSTEM PERFORMANCE METRICS', 'KEY STATISTICS', 'BY THE NUMBERS' sections filled with invented data, and 'LABEL // YEAR' micro-formatting ('SYSTEM // 2024', 'METRICS // 2025'), are lazy AI conventions. Never fabricate metrics; when real data is missing use an explicit placeholder like [metric], not invented numbers.

matcher.pattern: BY THE NUMBERS|KEY STATISTICS|SYSTEM PERFORMANCE METRICS|METRICS //|SYSTEM //|[A-Z][A-Z ]{3,} // [0-9]{4}

source.rule: No fake system/metric sections... If real data is not available, use clear placeholder labels like [metric] instead of making up numbers
No LABEL // YEAR formatting — 'SYSTEM // 2024', 'METRICS // 2025' is a lazy AI convention

tests.label: placeholder convention passes
tests.input: The stat card shows a labelled `[metric]` placeholder until real numbers arrive.

notes: ZS-UI-070 covers invented stat rows generally; this targets the metric-section trope and the double-slash micro-format. The [metric] placeholder convention is the allowed alternative to fabrication.

title: Custom mouse cursors
summary: Custom mouse cursors (cursor: url(...)) are outdated, accessibility-hostile, and perf-hostile — they break pointer affordances and add zero information. Use native cursors or none.

source.rule: NO custom mouse cursors. Outdated, accessibility-hostile, perf-hostile.

title: Figures without tabular numerals (data columns / density >7)
summary: Numbers in proportional type jitter as they change — columns shift, totals wobble. Data columns and stat-heavy dashboards (density > 7) must use tabular figures (font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums) or monospace so digits stay aligned.

source.rule: High-Density Override: When density exceeds 7, all numbers must use Monospace
Numbers in proportional font. Use a monospace font or enable tabular figures (font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums) for data-heavy interfaces

tests.label: proportional figures fail
tests.input: A table of prices and counts renders `1,234.50` in a proportional font — the digits shift column as they update.

tests.label: tabular figures pass
tests.input: Stat columns use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`; the density-9 dashboard renders all numbers in mono.

title: Vague labels (Overview / Insights) where specific language is possible
summary: Vague labels — 'Overview', 'Insights', 'Analytics' — where specific language is possible mark the UI as template-built. Name nav items and sections for their contents ('Progress', 'Library', 'Refunds', 'Market fit'), not generic umbrellas.

source.rule: Vague labels such as 'Overview,' 'Insights,' or 'Learn more' where specific language is possible
Direct, specific labels beat safe generic ones. Name nav items for their contents ('Progress', 'Library'), not vague umbrellas ('Home')

notes: 'Learn more' is already covered by ZS-UI-066 (generic CTAs).

title: Letter-spacing: one value for all sizes
summary: Tracking is size-specific, never one value: large display text wants negative tracking (letters read too far apart as they grow), small text wants slightly positive tracking for legibility. A single letter-spacing applied to every size is wrong somewhere; tighten headings, leave body near 0.

source.rule: Tracking (letter-spacing) is size-specific — never one value for all sizes

tests.label: fixed tracking fails
tests.input: A global `letter-spacing: 0.02em` on every heading size — display text reads airy, small labels cramped.

tests.label: size-specific tracking passes
tests.input: Display uses `-0.02em` at clamp(2rem, 5vw, 4rem); body stays near 0; captions get +0.02em.
